**Feasibility Limits of Rhenium-Based Hypervelocity Momentum Transfer for Small Orbital Debris Removal**

Bakhyt Zhakanov a, Karim Aubakirov a

*a Independent Researcher*

Corresponding author: Bakhyt Zhakanov (email address to be provided at submission)

# **Abstract**

**Background:** Small (1–10 cm) orbital debris is untrackable by current surveillance networks yet poses significant collision risk in low Earth orbit (LEO). A proposed remediation concept — hypervelocity impact of a dispersed rhenium projectile cloud — has been suggested as a means of imparting deorbiting momentum to such objects without requiring individual tracking or rendezvous.

**Purpose:** This study presents a constraint-driven, thirteen-simulation feasibility analysis of the rhenium-cloud concept, built around explicit physical falsification gates, full reporting of unfavorable results, and an explicit traceability tag (derived, sourced, or unvalidated) on every quantitative input.

**Methods:** Projectile mass requirements are derived from first-principles orbital momentum balance; the NASA Standard Breakup Model is applied as a catastrophic-fragmentation falsification gate; cloud dispersion (Clohessy–Wiltshire relative motion) is coupled directly into a terminal guidance hit-probability model; orbital decay is integrated using the NRLMSISE-00 empirical atmosphere; and aggregate uncertainty is propagated via 10⁶-sample Monte Carlo simulation with Sobol sensitivity decomposition.

**Results:** At a representative operating point (800 km, momentum enhancement β \= 1.5, 10 cm aluminum target), the design-mass projectile ratio required to guarantee deorbiting impulse (f(h) ≈ 0.42 g rhenium per g aluminum, including a 2× safety margin) yields a specific impact energy of 80 kJ/kg — twice the 40 kJ/kg NASA Standard Breakup Model catastrophic-disruption threshold — producing an estimated 443 new trackable fragments per engagement (net debris increase of 442 objects). Terminal guidance hit probability collapses to effectively zero (P\_hit ≈ 6×10⁻⁵⁸) at realistic control-loop latencies (≥10 ms). Gross engagement cost is estimated at ≥$163,500/kg even under favorable assumptions, before accounting for the fragmentation-adjusted cost per kilogram of debris actually removed, which is formally undefined because net debris removal is negative. Joint Monte Carlo propagation across all modeled uncertainty (10⁶ samples) yields a probability of simultaneous viability of 0.0000%.

**Conclusions:** Momentum-transfer deorbiting via a rhenium hypervelocity cloud, as specified, is not physically or economically viable for centimeter-scale LEO debris remediation. The dominant constraint is structural: the projectile mass margin required to guarantee deorbiting impulse is itself sufficient to place every credible design point in the catastrophic fragmentation regime, independent of the guidance and cost constraints that separately and independently falsify the concept. Tungsten is identified as a materially superior projectile material candidate should any momentum-transfer variant be pursued.

**Keywords:** orbital debris removal; hypervelocity impact; fragmentation risk; momentum transfer; rhenium; feasibility analysis

# **1\. Introduction**

Small orbital debris — objects between roughly 1 and 10 cm in characteristic length — represents a disproportionate collision hazard in low Earth orbit (LEO) because it lies below the reliable tracking threshold of ground-based surveillance networks (approximately 10 cm in LEO) while retaining sufficient mass and closing velocity (typically 7–15 km/s) to catastrophically damage or destroy operational spacecraft on impact \[1\]. Because these objects cannot be individually cataloged, conventional active debris removal (ADR) approaches — robotic capture, net or harpoon rendezvous, electrodynamic tethers — which require a tracked, targetable object, are not directly applicable to this size class \[2,3\].

This has motivated interest in remediation concepts that do not require individual tracking: instead, a dispersed cloud of small, dense projectiles is placed on a converging trajectory with a debris-populated orbital shell, and momentum transfer from hypervelocity impact is used to lower the perigee of intercepted objects below the threshold for atmospheric reentry. Rhenium — the forth-densest naturally stable element after osmium — has been proposed as a projectile material on the premise that higher density improves momentum-transfer efficiency per unit projectile volume.

Momentum-transfer debris remediation concepts of this type are, however, particularly susceptible to a specific class of methodological failure: because the interception geometry, the fraction of a dispersed cloud that actually strikes a given target, and the resulting momentum coupling are difficult to measure directly, early-stage analyses of this concept class have a documented tendency to substitute an assumed, unsourced interception-efficiency factor for a physically derived one; to apply catastrophic-disruption thresholds — such as the NASA Standard Breakup Model's 40 kJ/kg criterion — inconsistently or not at all; and to report only the subset of constituent simulations that support a favorable conclusion, omitting cost, guidance-feasibility, and fragmentation analyses that may contradict it. Any credible feasibility assessment of this concept class must therefore be built around explicit falsification gates and full reporting of unfavorable results, rather than around a single favorable headline calculation.

The present study reports a constraint-driven feasibility analysis of the rhenium-cloud momentum-transfer concept, structured around this principle. We (i) eliminate any assumed interception-efficiency factor, deriving required projectile mass entirely from first-principles orbital momentum balance; (ii) apply the NASA Standard Breakup Model as a hard falsification gate evaluated before any downstream design work, rather than as a post-hoc check; (iii) use established, queryable physical models — NRLMSISE-00 for atmospheric density, Fay–Riddell theory for reentry heating — rather than fitted or hand-tuned approximations; (iv) report all thirteen constituent simulations in this analysis, including every unfavorable result; and (v) tag every quantitative input with an explicit traceability status — derived from stated physics, sourced to a specific citation, or flagged as an unvalidated engineering assumption — so that the evidentiary basis for each numerical claim is auditable independent of the surrounding prose.

Section 2 describes the governing physics and the constraint-driven simulation architecture. Section 3 presents results organized by the specific research questions the analysis was designed to answer. Section 4 discusses the structural implications of the central finding — that the safety margin required for a viable deorbiting impulse is itself sufficient to force catastrophic fragmentation — for the broader class of momentum-transfer debris remediation concepts. Section 5 concludes.

# **2\. Material and methods**

## **2.1 Analytical framework and falsification-gate philosophy**

The analysis is organized as a sequence of thirteen linked simulations (SIM-0 through SIM-12), each addressing a distinct physical, engineering, or economic sub-question, with outputs from earlier simulations feeding as inputs to later ones. Unlike a conventional forward-design workflow, the analysis is deliberately falsification-first: SIM-0 establishes the hard physical boundary within which any design must operate (Section 2.2) before any projectile, guidance, or platform sizing is performed. If no design point exists that simultaneously satisfies this boundary and the deorbiting requirement, this is reported as a primary result rather than assumed away.

Every quantitative input is assigned one of three traceability tags: DERIVED (obtained by algebraic or numerical derivation from stated, non-controversial physics); SOURCED (obtained from a specific, cited published source); or UNVALIDATED (an engineering assumption for which no direct experimental or literature source exists at the relevant length- and velocity-scale). This convention is carried through Sections 2 and 3 and is summarized for major inputs in Table 1\.

## **2.2 Catastrophic disruption boundary and momentum-balance mass scaling**

For a target debris object of mass m\_t in a circular orbit at altitude h, the apogee-impulse velocity change required to lower perigee to a target reentry altitude h\_p (100 km) is obtained from the vis-viva equation:

*Δvdeorbit(h) \= √\[μ/(RE\+h)\]  −  √{μ\[2/(RE\+h) − 2/(2RE\+h+hp)\]}     (1)*

where μ is Earth's gravitational parameter and R\_E is Earth's mean radius \[DERIVED — standard Keplerian mechanics\].

Momentum conservation for a projectile of mass m\_p striking the target at relative velocity v\_rel, with a momentum-enhancement factor β accounting for ejecta-augmented coupling, gives:

*mt · Δvdeorbit  \=  β · mp · vrel     (2)*

Solving for the minimum required projectile mass and substituting into the specific-energy definition E\_s \= 0.5 m\_p v\_rel² / m\_t (the governing quantity in the NASA Standard Breakup Model \[4\]) yields:

*Es(h, vrel, β)  \=  Δvdeorbit(h) · vrel / (2β)     (3)*

Equation (3) is used, prior to any projectile sizing, to compute the maximum relative velocity v\_max,safe at which a given altitude can be engaged without exceeding the NASA Standard Breakup Model's catastrophic-disruption threshold E\_s,c (30–50 kJ/kg, central value 40 kJ/kg \[4\]):

*vmax,safe(h,β)  \=  2 Es,c β / Δvdeorbit(h)     (4)*

The momentum-enhancement factor β has no confirmed source specific to solid-metal, centimeter-scale, sub-orbital-velocity impacts; it is therefore treated as a flat, uniform UNVALIDATED distribution over \[1.0, 2.5\] throughout the analysis, rather than fixed at a single value or fitted to an unverifiable regression.

Required projectile mass is computed with an explicit engineering safety margin γ \= 2:

*mp,design  \=  γ · mp,min  \=  γ Δvdeorbit(h) mt / (β vrel)     (5)*

and the resulting design mass ratio f(h) \= m\_p,design/m\_t is independent of target mass (Section 3.4). Target debris mass is computed as a solid aluminum 6061 sphere (ρAl \= 2.70 g/cm³ \[5\]) for consistency across all downstream simulations.

## **2.3 Orbital decay modeling**

Post-engagement orbital lifetime — for successfully deorbited debris (perigee lowered to 100 km) and for rhenium mass that misses its intended target and remains on its original near-circular trajectory — is obtained by numerically integrating

*da/dt  \=  −CD (A/m) ρ(h) √(μ a)     (6)*

for near-circular orbits, and by full three-dimensional Cartesian propagation (including atmospheric co-rotation) for the eccentric post-impulse debris orbit, which passes through several orders of magnitude of density variation per revolution. Atmospheric density ρ(h) is obtained directly from the NRLMSISE-00 empirical atmosphere model \[6\], evaluated across solar-minimum, nominal, and solar-maximum conditions (F10.7 \= 70, 150, 250). Model output was cross-checked against the documented decay history of Starshine 1 (NORAD ID 25769; 387 km circular orbit, 258-day observed lifetime \[7,8\]), yielding an under-prediction of 34%, consistent with the expected ±30–50% uncertainty band for empirical density models driven by averaged rather than daily solar/geomagnetic indices.

## **2.4 Cloud dispersion and terminal guidance**

Following projectile release, the spatial evolution of the dispersed cloud is modeled using linearized Clohessy–Wiltshire relative motion in the Hill frame \[9\]:

*δz(t) \= (δvlaunch/n) sin(nt),   δx(t) \= (2δvlaunch/n)(1−cos(nt)),   δy(t) \= (3δvlaunch/n)(nt − sin(nt))     (7)*

where n \= √(μ/a³) is orbital mean motion and δv\_launch is the velocity dispersion imparted at release (UNVALIDATED — no experimental basis exists for converting a solid rhenium projectile into a uniform grain/dust swarm at the modeled scales). The resulting cloud angular half-width, evaluated at the time-of-flight corresponding to the terminal engagement range R, is passed directly as the effective target cross-section σ\_cloud into the terminal hit-probability model, rather than being treated as an independent, assumed cone angle:

*σpos(R) \= (λ/D) R,   dmiss \= √\[σpos² \+ (vrelτ)²\],   Phit(R) \= exp\[−dmiss²/(2σcloud²)\]     (8)*

where λ/D is the diffraction-limited angular resolution of a stated optical sensor aperture \[10\] and τ is terminal guidance control-loop latency.

## **2.5 Fragmentation modeling**

The NASA Standard Breakup Model \[4\] cumulative fragment-count relation

*N(Lc)  \=  0.1 M^0.75 Lc^−1.71,   Lc \> 1 mm     (9)*

is applied with the regime-dependent effective mass M set equal to the total colliding mass (mt \+ mp) whenever Es ≥ Es,c (catastrophic regime), the regime that applies at every credible design point identified in Section 3.1. Net debris flux is computed as one object removed minus the number of new fragments at or above 1 cm generated by the impact.

## **2.6 Electromagnetic launch envelope**

Required launcher electrical energy and physical scale are computed from standard coilgun/railgun energy relations (E\_kin \= 0.5 m\_p v², E\_elec \= E\_kin/η) and compared against three demonstrated benchmarks: a 3.2 kg projectile at 2,520–2,579 m/s (10.16–10.64 MJ, US Navy/ONR, 2008\) \[11\], a 3 g projectile at 5,900 m/s \[12\], and a 10 g projectile at approximately 2,000 m/s \[13\].

## **2.7 Material trade study**

Rhenium is compared against tungsten, tantalum, structural steel, and copper on six metrics: momentum efficiency (identical across materials at fixed mass, since p \= mv is density-independent), unit cost, global annual production, oxide toxicity/volatility on reentry, orbital persistence (area-to-mass ratio of missed grains, A/m \= 3/(4ρr) for a sphere of radius r), and reentry ablation energy.

## **2.8 Reentry ablation and environmental assessment**

Peak stagnation-point convective heating is computed using rate-limited Fay–Riddell theory \[14\], q\_w \= k√(ρ\_∞/R\_n) v\_∞³, rather than a total-energy ablation budget, since reentry heating is rate-limited rather than energy-limited. Ablated mass fraction, surviving ballistic coefficient, and ground casualty expectation (compared against the NASA 10⁻⁴ per-event threshold) are computed for both target debris and missed projectile material.

## **2.9 Cost-economic model**

Gross cost per kilogram of target mass engaged is computed as

*C\_gross  \=  C\_shot / \[m\_t · max(P\_hit, 10⁻⁶)\]     (10)*

where C\_shot aggregates rhenium material cost, launch cost, and amortized platform cost. Because net debris removal is negative at every catastrophic-regime design point (Section 3.6), the fragmentation-adjusted cost per kilogram of debris actually removed is formally undefined and is reported as such rather than substituted with a finite approximation. Rhenium price is drawn from USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025–2026 ($2,600–$7,280/kg) \[15\]; launch cost spans dedicated-launch ($3,000/kg) to small-payload rideshare-marginal ($7,000/kg) pricing \[16\]. Competitor remediation cost benchmarks are drawn from published cost assessments \[17,18,19\].

## **2.10 Regulatory compliance assessment**

The full post-engagement population — original debris, catastrophic fragments (Section 2.5), and missed projectile mass (Section 2.3) — is evaluated against the FCC 5-year post-mission disposal rule \[20\], the NASA Orbital Debris Mitigation Standard Practices 25-year guideline \[21\], and IADC net-debris-flux guidance, using orbital lifetime data read directly from the SIM-2 and SIM-5 outputs at runtime to preserve a single source of truth across the pipeline.

## **2.11 Platform mass budget**

A representative transporter spacecraft mass budget (structure, avionics, power, electromagnetic launcher, propulsion, thermal control) is developed using standard subsystem mass-fraction estimation and the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation for propellant sizing, for two end-of-life scenarios: direct deorbiting burn and rendezvous with an orbital replenishment hub.

## **2.12 Global uncertainty quantification**

All parameters carrying a stated uncertainty range (Table 1\) are propagated jointly through the full analysis pipeline via Monte Carlo sampling (10⁶ draws, fixed random seed for reproducibility), rather than via one-at-a-time sensitivity sweeps, which do not correctly characterize variance in a nonlinear, multi-constraint system \[22\]. Overall viability is defined as the joint satisfaction of five constraints: non-catastrophic specific energy, non-trivial hit probability (P\_hit \> 0.01), compliant orbital lifetime of missed material (≤25 years), non-negative net debris flux, and cost below $100,000 per kilogram of debris removed. Sobol first-order and total sensitivity indices \[23\] are computed to identify the dominant sources of output variance.

# **3\. Results**

## **3.1 Viability boundary and the central structural finding**

Evaluating Equation (4) across the tested altitude range (200–1200 km) and the full momentum-enhancement envelope (β ∈ \[1.0, 2.5\]) shows that the maximum relative velocity permissible before catastrophic disruption falls rapidly with altitude (Fig. 1; Table 2). At 800 km, v\_max,safe ranges from 412.8 m/s (β=1.0) to 1032.0 m/s (β=2.5), against a central value of 619.2 m/s at β=1.5. Typical LEO relative encounter velocities (7.5–15 km/s) exceed this ceiling by one to two orders of magnitude at any tested altitude or β value.

**Central structural finding.** Applying the required engineering safety margin (γ=2, Eq. 5\) to the minimum projectile mass necessary to guarantee sufficient deorbiting impulse produces a design-point specific energy of exactly double the value used to define the safe boundary: at h=800 km, β=1.5, a 10 cm aluminum target, the minimum-mass design point sits at E\_s \= 40.0 kJ/kg by construction, while the design mass actually required to provide operational margin (m\_p,design \= 2 m\_p,min) yields E\_s \= 80.0 kJ/kg — exactly twice the NASA Standard Breakup Model catastrophic threshold. This is a direct algebraic consequence of E\_s scaling linearly with delivered projectile mass at fixed target mass and velocity (Eq. 3): any finite engineering safety margin on projectile mass necessarily and proportionally pushes the specific impact energy past the catastrophic-disruption threshold that the margin-free design point was constructed to satisfy. A viable design point with both (a) sufficient margin to reliably provide the required deorbiting impulse and (b) impact energy safely below the disruption threshold does not exist within this analysis's momentum-balance framework. This finding is independent of, and structurally prior to, the terminal guidance and cost constraints discussed in Sections 3.5 and 3.10.

![][image1]

Fig. 1\. Maximum safe relative intercept velocity as a function of altitude across the tested momentum-enhancement envelope (β \= 1.0–2.5) and disruption-threshold range (30–50 kJ/kg). The safe zone narrows rapidly with altitude and lies one to two orders of magnitude below representative LEO closing velocities at every tested altitude.

## **3.2 Deorbit sufficiency and orbital lifetime**

Where a hypothetical impact within the safe zone is achieved, the resulting perigee-lowering is highly effective: post-impulse debris orbits (perigee 100 km) decay within approximately 49–190 minutes across the tested target size range (1–10 cm) and solar activity conditions, confirming that the deorbiting mechanism itself is physically adequate once achieved (Table 3).

## **3.3 Altitude ceiling**

The operationally relevant altitude ceiling is jointly constrained by the narrowing safe-velocity envelope (Section 3.1) and by the orbital persistence of projectile mass that misses its intended target. Missed rhenium grains at 800 km with diameter ≥0.5 mm persist in orbit for 9.11 to 36.43 years across the tested solar activity range — exceeding the FCC 5-year disposal threshold in all cases and the NASA 25-year threshold at the upper end. Above approximately 600–800 km, essentially all tested missed-grain sizes violate at least one applicable orbital-lifetime regulation, independent of the fragmentation and cost constraints identified separately below.

## **3.4 Mass ratio requirements and distance-independence**

The design mass ratio f(h) \= m\_p,design/m\_t is, by construction, independent of target mass and of terminal engagement range R — it depends only on altitude (via Δv\_deorbit) and the momentum-enhancement factor β. At h=800 km, f(h) ranges from 0.150 (β=2.5) to 0.939 (β=1.0), with a central value of 0.417 g Re/g Al at β=1.5 (Table 3). This distance-independence is a non-obvious consequence of momentum balance: while the required mass ratio does not depend on R, the probability of achieving a hit at all is entirely a function of R and is addressed separately in Section 3.5.

## **3.5 Cloud dispersion and terminal guidance — negative finding**

Coupling the Clohessy–Wiltshire cloud-dispersion model (Section 2.4) directly into the terminal hit-probability calculation, rather than assuming an independent cone angle, shows that control-loop latency dominates miss distance at every tested engagement range. At a representative engagement (R \= 10 m, v\_rel \= 619.2 m/s), a 1 ms control lag yields a marginally viable hit probability (P\_hit \= 0.268), but this collapses to effective machine-zero (P\_hit ≈ 6.3×10⁻⁵⁸) at a 10 ms lag — a latency well within the range of realistic terminal guidance actuator response — because the resulting positional drift (v\_rel·τ ≈ 6.2 m) is more than an order of magnitude larger than the cloud's own cross-section at intercept (σ\_cloud ≈ 0.38 m) (Fig. 2). Reliable terminal engagement of centimeter-scale debris at the velocities required for non-catastrophic momentum transfer is not achievable with control-loop latencies above roughly 1 ms, which is at the current limit of demonstrated terminal reaction-control technology.

![][image2]

Fig. 2\. Terminal hit probability collapses by more than 50 orders of magnitude between 1 ms and 10 ms control-loop latency at a fixed 619.2 m/s intercept velocity, driven by the linear growth of positional drift with latency relative to a near-fixed cloud cross-section.

## **3.6 Fragmentation — negative finding**

Applying the NASA Standard Breakup Model at the design-point specific energy identified in Section 3.1 (E\_s \= 80 kJ/kg, catastrophic regime, effective mass M \= m\_t \+ m\_p) to a representative 10 cm aluminum target at 800 km yields approximately 443 new trackable fragments (L\_c ≥ 1 cm) per successful engagement — a net debris increase of 442 objects for the removal of a single target (Fig. 3; Table 4). This holds across every tested altitude and target size within the catastrophic regime identified in Section 3.1, and constitutes, independent of the guidance constraint in Section 3.5, a second and independently sufficient basis on which the concept as specified fails to achieve its stated remediation objective.

![][image3]

Fig. 3\. Net trackable-object flux (objects removed minus fragments created) is strongly negative across all tested altitudes and target sizes in the catastrophic disruption regime, indicating the concept generates substantially more debris than it removes at every credible design point.

## **3.7 Electromagnetic launch technology assessment**

The projectile mass and velocity required at the representative 800 km, β=1.5 design point (590 g at 619.2 m/s; kinetic energy 113.1 kJ, electrical energy 282.7 kJ at 40% coilgun efficiency) lies well within the envelope of demonstrated electromagnetic launch technology (10.16–10.64 MJ demonstrated at 2,520–2,579 m/s for a 3.2 kg projectile \[11\]). Launch technology is therefore not an independent limiting constraint at the velocities identified as physically safe in Section 3.1 — though this same technological adequacy also makes the higher, catastrophic-regime velocities required elsewhere in the analysis technologically achievable, rather than naturally self-limiting.

## **3.8 Material trade study**

Because momentum (p \= mv) is independent of projectile density at fixed mass, rhenium's core proposed justification — exceptional density — confers no momentum-transfer advantage over lower-density alternatives; density affects only projectile grain size for a given mass. On cost and availability, tungsten (19.25 g/cm³, 91.6% of rhenium's density) is available at approximately 1/50th to 1/100th of rhenium's per-kilogram cost and at roughly 1,000 times the annual global production volume (Table 5; Fig. 4). Rhenium is not materially justified as a projectile material for this application on any of the six evaluated metrics.

![][image4]

Fig. 4\. Material trade-study comparison. Rhenium occupies a dominated position relative to tungsten on cost and availability, while offering no momentum-coupling advantage from its higher density.

## **3.9 Reentry ablation and environmental impact**

Target debris and missed projectile material at or below approximately 1 cm diameter fully ablate during reentry under Fay–Riddell rate-limited heating; objects of 2 cm and larger partially survive to ground impact. Ground casualty expectation for surviving objects remains below the NASA 10⁻⁴ per-event threshold (≤2.5×10⁻⁵) across the tested size range. Annual atmospheric deposition of rhenium heptoxide (Re₂O₇) from missed material is estimated at approximately 1 kg/yr, several orders of magnitude below natural cosmic dust influx.

## **3.10 Cost-economic analysis — negative finding**

Gross cost per kilogram of target mass engaged, even under the most favorable tested combination of parameters (1 ms control lag, P\_hit \= 0.268, USGS-floor rhenium pricing, dedicated-launch pricing), is estimated at approximately $163,500/kg, rising to approximately $187,000/kg under rideshare-marginal launch pricing (Table 6; Fig. 5). Under the nominal, nearer-realistic control lag (10 ms or greater), hit probability collapses (Section 3.5) and gross cost per kilogram becomes effectively unbounded. Because net debris removal is negative at every catastrophic-regime design point (Section 3.6), cost per kilogram of debris actually removed from orbit is formally undefined rather than merely large. For context, published cost estimates for alternative small-debris remediation approaches range from approximately $100–$500/kg (ground-based laser ablation) to $10,000–$100,000/kg (active debris removal tugs) \[17,18,19\] — the rhenium-cloud concept's best-case gross cost already exceeds the upper end of this competitive range before any fragmentation penalty is applied.

![][image5]

Fig. 5\. Best-case gross cost per kilogram of target mass engaged for the rhenium-cloud concept exceeds published cost estimates for every competing small-debris remediation approach, before accounting for the additional (formally undefined) penalty from net-negative debris removal.

## **3.11 Regulatory compliance**

The full post-engagement population (surviving debris, catastrophic fragments, missed projectile mass) fails the FCC 47 CFR 25.283 five-year disposal rule and conditionally fails the NASA ODMSP 25-year guideline, driven by both missed-grain persistence (Section 3.3) and secondary fragment lifetime (\~15 years, Section 3.6). The concept fails IADC net-debris-flux guidance outright, given the negative net flux identified in Section 3.6. Aircraft-strike risk within a required NOTAM exclusion corridor (1,000 × 100 km) is estimated at 5×10⁻⁷ per event, requiring 24-hour advance notice under FAA convention (Table 7).

## **3.12 Platform design**

A representative transporter spacecraft mass budget totals approximately 630 kg dry mass (structure, avionics, power, electromagnetic launcher, propulsion, thermal control) plus a 50 kg rhenium payload, supporting on the order of 85 design-point shots per reload cycle. End-of-life analysis indicates a propellant-remaining threshold of 42.9 kg (equal to the direct-deorbit propellant requirement from 800 km) below which rendezvous with an orbital replenishment hub, rather than direct deorbiting, is the appropriate disposal strategy.

## **3.13 Global viability probability**

Propagating all stated parameter uncertainty jointly through the full analysis pipeline via 10⁶-sample Monte Carlo simulation yields an overall probability of simultaneous viability — non-catastrophic specific energy, non-trivial hit probability, compliant orbital lifetime, non-negative net debris flux, and sub-$100,000/kg cost, all evaluated together — of 0.0000% (0 of 1,000,000 samples). Individual constraint pass rates are: non-catastrophic impact, 2.89%; non-trivial hit probability, 0.25%; compliant missed-grain decay, 96.07%; non-negative net debris flux, 2.89%; sub-$100,000/kg cost, 0.00% (Fig. 6). Sobol sensitivity decomposition attributes the dominant share of output variance to terminal guidance control lag (68.0%), followed by intercept velocity (18.0%), momentum-enhancement factor β (7.0%), launch cost (4.0%), rhenium price (2.0%), and target mass (1.0%) (Fig. 7).

# **4\. Discussion**

## **4.1 The structural margin-disruption finding as the primary falsification mechanism**

The central result of this analysis (Section 3.1) is not that the rhenium-cloud concept fails at some unfortunate combination of otherwise-independent parameters, but that it fails structurally: the requirement for any finite engineering safety margin on projectile mass is in direct algebraic conflict with the requirement to remain below the catastrophic-disruption threshold, because both the deorbiting impulse and the disruption risk scale with the same delivered momentum. A margin-free design point exists exactly at the disruption boundary (Section 3.1), which is itself not an engineering design — a system with zero mass margin against manufacturing tolerance, aiming error, or grain loss cannot be relied upon to deliver the intended impulse. This structural tension is not resolvable by re-tuning any single input parameter within the momentum-balance framework used here; it would require either a fundamentally different coupling mechanism, in which deorbiting impulse and disruption risk do not scale together, or an acceptance that routine, deliberate fragmentation is an intended outcome of the concept rather than a side effect to be avoided (Section 4.3).

## **4.2 Independent, compounding falsifications**

Sections 3.5, 3.6, and 3.10 identify three further, mutually independent bases on which the concept as specified fails to achieve viability: terminal guidance control-loop latency at realistic values collapses hit probability to effective zero; the catastrophic disruption identified in Section 4.1 independently generates substantially more trackable debris than it removes; and gross cost per kilogram of target mass engaged exceeds even the most expensive competing remediation technology before the undefined fragmentation penalty is applied. The joint Monte Carlo viability probability of 0.0000% (Section 3.13) reflects the near non-overlap of the parameter regions in which each of these four constraints — energy, guidance, debris flux, and cost — is independently satisfied, rather than a single narrow failure mode. A concept that fails on four independent physical and economic grounds simultaneously is substantially less likely to be rescued by refinement of any one subsystem than a concept failing on a single margin.

## **4.3 Conditions under which viability could be reconsidered**

Three re-scoping directions follow directly from the structural finding in Section 4.1 and are worth stating explicitly, since none is foreclosed by this analysis. First, deliberate, budgeted fragmentation: if the concept is reframed as a controlled fragmentation-and-decay strategy — accepting that catastrophic disruption is the intended mechanism rather than an avoided side effect — the relevant design question becomes whether the resulting fragment population decays within regulatory timeframes faster than the original intact object would have, which is a different and not-yet-answered question from the one addressed here. Second, sub-catastrophic, low-margin operation: operating strictly at or below the margin-free boundary avoids catastrophic disruption but removes the engineering margin this analysis treats as a minimum requirement, and would require independent, non-mass-based means of ensuring reliable impulse delivery. Third, sub-millisecond terminal guidance: the guidance falsification in Section 3.5 is latency-dominated; actuator and sensing architectures capable of sub-millisecond terminal correction, if developed, would independently address this constraint without altering the energy-margin finding in Section 4.1. None of these directions is evaluated further in this study; each represents a substantively different concept requiring its own dedicated feasibility analysis.

## **4.4 Material selection implications**

Independent of the viability findings above, the material trade study (Section 3.8) indicates that rhenium's proposed justification — high density improving momentum-transfer efficiency — does not hold, since momentum at fixed mass is density-independent. Should any momentum-transfer variant of this concept be pursued under one of the re-scoped directions in Section 4.3, tungsten offers materially better cost and availability characteristics with no momentum-coupling penalty, and would warrant evaluation ahead of rhenium in any follow-on design.

## **4.5 Methodological contribution**

Beyond the specific feasibility result, this analysis illustrates a general methodological approach for constraint-driven evaluation of proposed debris remediation concepts: establishing physical falsification gates prior to downstream design work, coupling models that are physically dependent on one another (Section 2.4) rather than treating them as independent inputs, reporting unfavorable simulation results with the same prominence as favorable ones, and tagging every quantitative claim with an explicit traceability status. We suggest this general approach — falsification-first, fully reported, traceability-tagged — as applicable to the evaluation of other early-stage, non-tracking-dependent debris remediation concepts more broadly.

## **4.6 Limitations**

This analysis inherits several stated modeling limitations. The momentum-enhancement factor β has no confirmed source specific to solid-metal, centimeter-scale, sub-orbital-velocity impacts and is treated as a flat, unvalidated uncertainty envelope (Section 2.2); a validated value could shift the specific quantitative boundaries in Section 3.1, though it would not resolve the structural margin-disruption tension described in Section 4.1, which holds for any finite β. The cloud-dispersion model assumes an idealized single-point launch source and does not model the physical mechanism by which a solid projectile is converted into a functional grain or dust swarm at the relevant scales, which is itself an unvalidated engineering assumption. The equivalence between a single macroscopic impactor and N sequential micro-grain impacts of equal total mass, used throughout the momentum-balance and fragmentation analyses, is a modeling assumption rather than a validated result and has not been checked against swarm-impact literature. Finally, the specific mass-bifurcation form of the NASA Standard Breakup Model used in Section 2.5 is corroborated across multiple secondary sources but has not been independently verified against the primary published text at the level of individual page and equation numbers.

# **5\. Conclusions**

A constraint-driven, thirteen-simulation feasibility analysis of rhenium-cloud hypervelocity momentum transfer for small (1–10 cm) orbital debris remediation finds the concept, as specified, is not viable. The central and structurally prior finding is that the engineering safety margin required to reliably deliver sufficient deorbiting impulse necessarily forces the specific impact energy into the catastrophic-fragmentation regime defined by the NASA Standard Breakup Model, independent of any single parameter value; a design point combining adequate margin with sub-catastrophic impact energy does not exist within the momentum-balance framework evaluated here. This structural finding is further and independently compounded by terminal guidance control-loop latency collapsing hit probability to effective zero at realistic actuator response times, by the catastrophic disruption itself generating a net increase in trackable orbital debris at every credible design point, and by gross engagement cost exceeding published cost estimates for every competing small-debris remediation technology. Joint Monte Carlo propagation of all stated parameter uncertainty yields a probability of simultaneous viability of 0.0000% across 10⁶ samples. We identify tungsten as a materially superior projectile material candidate on cost and availability grounds, independent of the viability findings, and outline three specific re-scoping directions — deliberate fragmentation-and-decay design, sub-catastrophic low-margin operation, and sub-millisecond terminal guidance — that would each require independent, dedicated feasibility analysis and are not evaluated further here.
